The order established a 500% tariff on Russian goods and a possible 100% tariff on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump said he submitted a certification to Congress stating that issuing the waiver was in the United States’ national interests.
The order implements the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on September 18.

summary: On Thursday, October 15, 2026, 16-year-old John Griffin Jr. III attacked Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three children aged 5, 8, and 11 and one teacher before an armed bystander fatally shot him.

Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter and father, heard gunfire while driving home, pursued the gunman into the school, and killed him. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek credited Giamanco with having "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."

Law enforcement sources said the pump-action shotgun was purchased by Griffin's mother around August. Oregon law generally prohibits minors from possessing firearms, though exceptions exist for certain lawful uses.

Five-Year-Old Rhoam Summer was identified as one of the four victims mourned by families and residents. A 7-year-old child and another teacher remain hospitalized with critical injuries from the shooting.

Police Chief Mike Krantz said the investigation into the motive and the shooter's access to the weapon will take time. Authorities have not announced charges against family members and maintain a heavy police presence at the school.
title: Teen shooter who killed 4 at Oregon elementary school was a former student, police say

summary: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is departing after just five days on the job. President Donald Trump hinted at the exit on Friday, suggesting she "reconsider" the role following intense scrutiny over her legal credentials.

Scrutiny intensified after Zacharia admitted on Thursday she had not passed the bar exam. Her first press briefing on Tuesday lasted less than 15 minutes with only three questions, drawing criticism for stilted delivery and lack of preparedness.

During a Fox News interview on Thursday, Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her credentials. President Donald Trump later told reporters he had advised her, "You don't have to be treated this badly," defending her against media scrutiny.

Zacharia's exit marks the quickest departure for a Trump press secretary, surpassing Anthony Scaramucci's 10-day tenure. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called the resignation "a sign of failure in the Republican White House."

As November midterm elections draw closer, Democrats are seizing on the departure to criticize Republican White House staffing. Zacharia praised President Donald Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man," writing it was an honour to work for him.
title: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after just 5 days on the job

summary: On Thursday, a 16-year-old gunman forced entry into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three children ages 5, 8, and 11, plus one teacher, before dying inside, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Officers arrived at the campus at 1:02 p.m., minutes after dispatchers received reports of a shooter firing into a car outside the school. An armed community member who witnessed the suspect enter pursued him inside and shot him, authorities said.

Two additional victims—a seven-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher—remain hospitalized with critical injuries. The attack triggered an immediate facility-wide lockdown, with adjacent campuses also placed under precautionary lockdown.

Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook canceled classes districtwide Friday, while police directed families to Journey Church at 61303 S Highway 97 for reunification with students evacuated by bus.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the community member's intervention, saying the bystander's actions carry "a heavy emotional burden." The shooting marks the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today.
title: 4 Killed, Including 3 Children, in Oregon Elementary School Shooting; Suspect Also Dead

summary: President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the Pentagon will not livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, reversing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan to broadcast the event online.
Growing public opposition prompted the reversal, as Hegseth had originally proposed streaming the December 3 execution by firing squad to demonstrate America's response to terrorism.
Hasan, a former Army Major, killed 13 people and injured 32 in a 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, Texas; the execution remains scheduled to proceed by firing squad.

Immediate families of victims may still witness the execution in person, while President Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday that many "well meaning people would rather not watch him die" through streaming.

In his Truth Social post, Trump cited FBI communications between Hasan and Yemeni-American cleric Anwar al-Awlaki during President Barack Obama administration, though investigators previously concluded those emails posed no threat.
title: Trump, after bipartisan backlash, says Pentagon won't livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter

Officers responded to 2999 North Greenwich Road after KWCH reported that dozens of emergency vehicles arrived following a pickup truck allegedly driving onto the field, resulting in multiple injuries.

Police have not yet specified the number of people injured or the severity of their injuries, nor have authorities released identities or ages of those affected. Authorities confirmed there is no further ongoing threat.

Drivers are asked to stay away from the area of 29th and Greenwich Road while the investigation continues. Wichita Police indicated further updates will be released when additional information becomes available.

As this remains a developing story, officials continue gathering evidence to determine how the incident occurred. Newsweek has reached out to Wichita Police for additional details regarding the crash.
title: At least 2 dead after vehicle drives through soccer game in Wichita, Kansas: Police

The poll shows Stelson leading Perry 49% to 46% among likely voters in south-central Pennsylvania, placing the margin of lead within the survey's 5.6 percentage point margin of error.
The findings highlight a highly competitive rematch between the candidates, following Perry's narrow victory over Stelson by approximately one percentage point in the previous election cycle.
Campaign strategists note that shifting suburban demographics around Harrisburg and York continue to turn the traditionally conservative-leaning district into a critical battleground.
Polling analysts emphasize that high turnout and independent voters in Cumberland and Dauphin counties will be key factors in deciding the final outcome.
title: Democrats hope a rematch can dislodge Trump loyalist Perry in Pennsylvania

Intense Santa Ana winds and high temperatures drove the blaze, with forecasters reporting gusts of 50 to 70 mph that created a "high risk for large fires and rapid fire growth."
By Friday night, Fire Chief TJ McGovern of the Orange County Fire Authority ordered 16,000 residents to evacuate, while two firefighters were hospitalized with heat-related injuries.

Authorities shut down power lines to prevent sparks, leaving more than 118,000 customers without electricity, while a separate Henderson fire burned at least 2,070 acres at the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton.
The National Weather Service expects dangerous fire conditions to persist through Saturday night, maintaining a heat advisory until 8pm Saturday for the Orange County and San Diego County coast.
title: Firefighters gain ground on Southern California blaze, allowing thousands to return home

Federal public health authorities additionally allocated nearly $4 million in emergency funding to strengthen contact tracing, community outreach, and vaccination access across affected counties.

summary: On Friday, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro launched New Path PAC, a federal political action committee designed to support four Democratic candidates in Pennsylvania's 1st, 7th, 8th, and 10th Congressional Districts.

Federal campaign finance laws prevent Shapiro from transferring his $60 million state-level war chest to federal races, making the new PAC necessary to directly support Democratic congressional candidates.

Political observers view the launch as Shapiro's "strongest signal yet" of a 2028 presidential run, mirroring recent federal PAC creations by Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and other prospective Democratic candidates.

During a debate last week, Shapiro declined to pledge a full four-year term as governor, insisting his "lone focus" remains flipping the House while attacking Donald Trump's "chaos, cruelty, and corruption."
Marshall Cohen, the PAC's executive director, stated the committee aims to help elect leaders who will "place a check on Donald Trump" and secure a Congressional majority this November.
title: Shapiro launches super PAC as presidential speculation mounts

More than 200 business executives will accompany Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. After Uzbekistan, he will visit Mumbai and Jamnagar, India, to meet Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani.
The trip occurs as the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis, and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations. Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state.
While Rubio focuses on Central Asia and India, other officials manage different foreign policy hotspots. Vance represented the United States in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
title: Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots

summary: On Friday, the FBI and CISA warned the American public to remain vigilant against AI-powered tricks ahead of next month's midterm elections, highlighting sophisticated tactics employed by malicious cyber criminals.
The alert noted that "super intelligence," a Trump-approved term for AI, is allowing hackers to sharpen rogue emails and text messages, making them appear more convincing to potential victims.

Fraudsters are deploying various schemes including fake PACs that collect donations, merchandise scams, and investment pools, often mimicking Campaign entity names and slogans to deceive supporters, the FBI reports.

Scammers are using phishing campaigns, sending text messages claiming recipients are not registered to vote to solicit personal data; the FBI advises verifying all political organizations via official government Elections websites.

While Texas Secretary of State Alicia Pierce confirmed a registration application backlog is cleared, Scammers may still leverage the incident to create urgency in deceptive phishing communications targeting Texans.
title: US tells election officials to be on guard against AI-powered tricks ahead of midterms

summary: The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating suspicious letters containing unidentified white powder sent to election offices nationwide, including Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon's office.

These incidents are part of an ongoing series of mailings targeting election officials and congressional offices across the United States, though federal authorities have not yet confirmed if the letters are connected.

Intercepted Friday before delivery, the Minnesota letter is undergoing testing by the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. Similar mailings triggered evacuations in Louisiana, Oklahoma, Arizona, and Wisconsin.

Senator Amy Klobuchar confirmed her office received a similar letter Friday, with no one in immediate danger. Election officials declared "Threats against election workers are unacceptable" and vowed not to be deterred.

With the general election less than three weeks away on Nov. 3, election officials are operating with a "war room mentality," coordinating security measures across all counties to protect voting integrity.
title: Letters with unidentified substance sent to Sen. Klobuchar, Rep. Morrison and Minnesota secretary of state

Strained by the ongoing Ukraine-Russia war and conflict in the Middle East, global energy supplies prompted the administration to implement these waivers to ease economic pressure.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the President plans a 60-day period to analyze economic impacts, while confirming a separate agreement for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel.

While the waiver offers relief to India, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy warned it could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Senator Darline Graham stated, "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled to be in India on Monday, October 19, 2026, as the administration weighs geopolitical consequences regarding pressure on Moscow.
title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions

summary: On Friday, President Donald Trump said normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia is "back on the table," noting Riyadh is "very happy" with Israeli and American support against Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

This security cooperation gained urgency after a missile strike on King Khalid International Airport last Saturday killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, forcing the kingdom to seek regional aid.

Earlier this week, American officials explored with IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir whether Israel could carry out direct strikes against the Houthis, though Zamir warned of potential regional escalation.

Saudi Arabia maintains that establishing diplomatic relations requires a credible path toward a sovereign Palestinian state, a condition that complicates the Abraham Accords' expansion despite current security alignment.

While Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office, progress remains difficult, as sources report Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed does not trust the Israeli leader, despite Trump's optimism about the Abraham Accords.
title: Trump says Saudi Arabia may accept Israeli help against Houthis, revive Abraham Accords

summary: On Friday, U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett warned President Donald Trump that failing to appear for his scheduled deposition could result in sanctions, including default judgment in the $10 billion BBC defamation suit.

Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion, alleging a 'false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction' of his January 6, 2021 speech; the BBC apologized for the edit but denies defaming the president.

Despite agreeing to an October 16 deposition, Trump's lawyers cancelled the session late last month, citing 'matters of national importance,' leaving the BBC unable to depose the 'most central figure' in the case.
Ordering a response by October 22, Magistrate Judge Lett warned that lawyers 'are not permitted to disregard the Court's orders and procedures,' with failure potentially resulting in sanctions.
Discovery concludes December 18, and Trump's team proposed pushing his testimony to January 2027, while the court expects 'strict compliance' to avoid sanctions before the deadline passes.
title: Judge Threatens to Sanction Trump Over Skipped Deposition in $10 Billion BBC Suit

ICE issued a "wanted" poster for Mendoza-Cervantes after the collision, but the man's daughter identified the photo as her father, Hector Jimenez Mendoza, who died in 2017.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, said it is "pretty obvious" from videos that ICE intentionally struck and ran over Parra, while ICE stated allegations are "RECKLESS and FALSE."

Cesar Espinosa, leader of FIEL Houston, called on ICE "to tell the truth" and release body camera footage, describing the deceased man's image use as "beyond mind-blowing.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, stated the coalition has shifted from protesting the second Trump administration to facilitating early voting, marking a strategic pivot for the coalition of about 200 partner organizations.

In Frisco, Texas, Indivisible Frisco co-leader Cammy Dunford plans a "voting is your superpower" gathering where volunteers trained by Common Cause will distribute 500 goodie bags with voting resources and serve as poll monitors.

Organizers cite concerns about the failed SAVE America Act and potential federal immigration officers at polling places as threats to election integrity, motivating groups to train poll watchers to protect voters during midterm elections.

title: Thousands of No Kings protests held for nationwide early voting ‘day of action’

President Donald Trump announced in September the structure would become a 'top grade' military complex with drone facilities and sniper positions, prompting alarm from aviation safety experts concerned about nearby airspace risks.

Interior Department spokesperson Katie Martin stated the arch design 'is capable of accommodating the national security functions' Trump highlighted, though the White House declined to release security details at this review stage.

Preservation League Executive Director Rebecca Miller warned that adding military components would require 'a new or supplemental review,' arguing it would violate federal obligations and disrupt Arlington's solemnity.

The National Capital Planning Commission will review the proposal at a Nov. 5 hearing, though experts note any future military components would require a separate regulatory process distinct from current approval track.
title: Final Trump arch plans submitted to city omit proposed military complex

Service disruptions affected subway lines as the station remained closed; MTA Chief Security Officer Michael Kemper said the perpetrator "should face maximum consequences from the justice system."

summary: On Monday, October 12, Homeland Security officers searched the Washington residence of Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar , seizing her phone and passport during an investigation into alleged immigration fraud.
Days before the search, Trump attacked Omar at a Tennessee rally, describing her home country of Somalia as a place of "crime and squalor" and suggesting Vice President Vance was investigating her.

Omar's legal team demanded the return of seized property, arguing there is "no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status.
title: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s lawyers say authorities ignored judge’s restrictions on home search

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Jewish and Muslim voters’ vulnerability, using “bitter,” “rattles,” and “on edge” to stress Gaza’s humanitarian, identity, and social consequences; right-leaning framing pivots toward whether Jewish Democrats can support Abdul El-Sayed, the potential first Muslim senator, and his gun-control campaign message, de-emphasizing Muslim voters in Dearborn.
Center coverage similarly calls the stakes “deeply personal” while avoiding overt partisan judgment.
The pivotal divide is whether Gaza and faith identity or candidate ideology and gun policy define the contest.
All perspectives portray a close race shaped by Gaza, religious concerns, and El-Sayed’s historic candidacy, reflecting wider cultural and geopolitical polarization.
summary: The Senate race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is testing Jewish and Arab American voters in Michigan amid deep divisions over the war in Gaza.

Tensions have escalated in the Detroit suburbs as voters confront personal questions about faith and identity, with communities shaken by Israel's war in Gaza and the March attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield.

To win over Jewish voters in Oakland County, Rogers has portrayed El-Sayed as an extremist, with allies repeatedly invoking claims he cannot condemn terrorism due to alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Arab American leaders who previously supported President Donald Trump are distancing themselves from Republican rhetoric, while Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud called such attacks on Muslim politicians 'very problematic.'
The rhetoric complicates efforts to unite Michigan voters, as Jewish Democratic activist Lori Goldman described the current climate as 'a fear campaign. It's spreading and it's not spreading slowly.
title: Michigan Senate Race Tests Jewish and Arab American Voters

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the agreement as “shining light” on a “long-lost” community, stressing recognition, marginalization, and Abadie’s Lebanese roots as an “integral part” of his identity; right-leaning coverage instead emphasizes cultural persistence, portraying his Arabic, French, music, and cuisine ties as evidence that Lebanese Jewish identity endures despite decline and absence, with only limited grounds to associate the headline with Israel’s legitimacy.
Center coverage adds intimate details—3,000 Arabic songs and his wife learning Lebanese cooking—without the left-right historical emphasis.
Across perspectives, the agreement itself is de-emphasized, while shared language and attention to heritage reveal a broader divide between restoration and continuity.
summary: Last month, Israel agreed to release five civilians detained in southern Lebanon in exchange for Lebanon's help searching for remains of Jewish leaders abducted during the 15-year civil war.
At least seven Jews are among the 17,000 missing Lebanese people since the conflict ended, including former community president Isac Sasson, doctor Elie Hallak, and secretary general Salim Jamous.
Though about 4,000 Jews remain on voting lists in Beirut and 1,000 in Sidon, attorney Bassem El Hout estimates only about 20 Jews are scattered across the country today.
Doron Spielman, spokesperson for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said Israel "has a profound and enduring responsibility to Jews throughout the world" which extends beyond Israel's borders.
Lebanese officials have not announced any breakthroughs in the search, and it remains unclear what will be done with any recovered remains if discovered.
title: Israel-Lebanon agreement shines light on long-lost Jewish community

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the Tampa talks chiefly as Beirut’s effort to halt “Israeli attacks,” invoking a “new war” involving Hezbollah and emphasizing a continued international security presence in southern Lebanon .

Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds “US-backed” diplomacy, a “framework agreement,” and alleged violations that obstruct Lebanese state-force deployment, portraying the issue through institutional and security obligations.
The center presents a more procedural middle ground, describing a scheduled meeting while retaining “attacks” or “escalation” through attribution.
The sharpest divide is whether the story centers Israeli responsibility and regional conflict or agreement enforcement and state authority.
All perspectives emphasize the October 20 trilateral talks, Aoun’s announcement, and persistent hostilities, reflecting broader geopolitical and sovereignty divides.
summary: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Lebanon and Israel will join U.S.-backed trilateral talks in Tampa, Florida, on October 20.
A Lebanese military delegation will present Beirut’s demands and seek an end to Israeli attacks, according to the Lebanese presidency.
Aoun reaffirmed support for extending the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon’s mandate and warned against a security vacuum in southern Lebanon.
The talks follow a U.S.-brokered framework involving Hezbollah’s disarmament and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces, while both sides remain at odds.
title: Lebanon says military delegation will press for halt to Israeli attacks at US talks

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the allegations as an escalating human-rights crisis, emphasizing a “surge,” “severely injuring,” 21 documented cases, and the Prison Service’s dismissal as a “smear campaign.” Center coverage retains attribution through “report,” but broadens the issue into “harsh treatment” and de-emphasizes case-specific evidence.

Right-Leaning coverage avoids “surge” and instead foregrounds graphic consequences—surgery, a fractured shin, and testicle removal—while portraying prisoners as “severely injured.” The pivotal divide is whether to stress systemic escalation, historical conditions, or individual harm, alongside whether official denial merits attention.

All perspectives nevertheless highlight close-range rubber-bullet shootings, serious injuries, and rights-group allegations, reflecting the conflict’s broader ideological divide over Israeli security and Palestinian rights.
summary: Israeli human rights groups have documented 22 cases of inmates shot with rubber bullets, reporting a surge in the practice that has become routine violence in prisons. One of the 22 detainees is Israeli; the rest are Palestinian.

Conditions in Israeli prisons deteriorated dramatically since the war in Gaza began more than three years ago. Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, authorities rounded up thousands of Palestinians, doubling the prison population to more than 9,000, according to Hamoked.

Medical records from Soroka document a 45-year-old inmate whose testicle was "completely crushed" by a rubber bullet, requiring surgical removal. Other detainees report being shot at point-blank range in cells, with several stating they received no medical treatment for resulting injuries.

Under Israel's prison regulations, guards may only use weapons when facing imminent risk, said Sari Bashi, executive director of the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel. However, the prison service's legal adviser defended the use of rubber bullets as "measured" and "appropriate."

Muhannad Abu Ghosh, director of the prisoners and detainees division at Physicians for Human Rights Israel, warned the practice is "becoming another routine form of violence." Rights groups urge the prison service to end behavior they call widespread and unlawful.
title: Israeli rights groups report a surge of Palestinian inmates being shot with rubber bullets

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames César Jáuregui’s arrest as a politically charged “ CIA agents’ controversy,” foregrounding tensions with Governor Maru Campos and terms like “narcolaboratory,” while de-emphasizing sovereignty and the deaths of two Americans.

Center and right perspectives stress alleged official misconduct and unauthorized foreign involvement, with “treason,” “US spies,” and “unauthorized CIA role” conveying secrecy, betrayal, and national-security anxiety; the right additionally notes that U.S. authorities did not confirm the CIA link.
Center coverage qualifies allegations with “accused,” but still highlights legal uncertainty.
All portray an arrest tied to a deadly anti-drug operation, reflecting broader divides over domestic politics, foreign intervention, and security.
summary: On Saturday, Mexican authorities arrested former Chihuahua Attorney General Cesar Jauregui on suspicion of treason, Attorney General Ernestina Godoy announced.
Prosecutors allege Jauregui allowed foreign agents to participate in an 'irregular' raid on a suspected drug laboratory in Chihuahua this April without required authorization under Mexican law.

The U.S. acknowledged in April that two employees of its embassy in Mexico City had died; sources identified them as CIA officers involved in anti-narcotics efforts, rekindling sensitivities around foreign involvement in Mexican security operations.

President Claudia Sheinbaum sought to de-escalate tensions, reiterating that Mexico welcomes intelligence sharing but does not permit foreign agents to participate directly in operations on Mexican territory.
Godoy stated a federal judge signed the arrest warrant following months of investigation; Jauregui could not immediately be reached for comment, and sources declined to comment on the case.
title: Ex-Chihuahua attorney general accused of treason for allowing US participation in drug raid

bias: All perspectives accept the reported transfers to the IRGC, but left-leaning coverage frames “cash-starved” Iran within a wider confrontation involving “immense pressure,” a naval blockade, and possible renewed combat, while right-leaning coverage treats the episode as proof of policy success, invoking “Iran broke?” alongside alleged $25 billion oil losses and $350 million in frozen cryptocurrency.

Center coverage emphasizes an “extraordinary reversal,” including militias allegedly withholding fighters’ salaries, while terms like “terror proxies,” “proxy forces,” and “terror network” sharpen negative portrayals across center and right.
The shared focus on financial strain and militia funding reflects broader divides over coercion, escalation, and Iran’s regional role.
summary: On Friday, CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper revealed that Iran-backed groups including Hezbollah, Hamas , and Shia militias in Iraq are sending money back to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to relieve economic pressure after nine months of war.

United States initiatives have severely strained Iran's economy; the naval blockade cost Iran $25 billion in oil revenue while the Treasury Department froze around $350 million in cryptocurrency assets to hinder weapons production.
Cooper attributed increased ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz to "desperation" within the IRGC, though the waterway remains open with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil transiting last week.

President Donald Trump stated on Thursday he would possibly use the "Mother of All Bombs," or MOAB, in future strikes against Iran, despite earlier indicating he would delay military action until after the November midterms.

While the White House and Qatari mediators await Iran's response to a United States counterproposal, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed on Friday that the Islamic Republic "will not bow to coercion" amid the ongoing conflict.
title: Iran-Backed Groups Sending Money to IRGC Amid Economic Pressure, US Says

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Eric Flores’s removal campaign as Republican discomfort with Trump, stressing voter confusion and legal escalation through phrases like “irked,” “sics lawyers,” and “boasting.” Center coverage instead portrays a Democratic-funded billboard as “fake” yet “free advertising,” emphasizing unauthorized imagery and strategic advantage.
Right-Leaning coverage is de-emphasized in the available analyses, so a direct contrast is limited.

The pivotal divide is whether Flores is distancing himself from Trump or resisting misleading campaign-like branding; left coverage also highlights ICE messaging, while center coverage foregrounds funding.
Across perspectives, the shared focus is the Brownsville billboard, its Trump association, and Flores’s demand for removal.
summary: On October 12, Republican congressional candidate Eric Flores demanded Lamar Advertising remove a digital billboard in Brownsville, Texas, arguing it mimics his campaign materials "to cause voter confusion."

The digital display prominently features a photo of Flores with President Donald Trump and his support for ICE; Democrats accuse Flores of hiding his Trump ties, though his campaign maintains the objection is solely about design.

Records identify Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez and the Northern Cameron County Democrats as sponsors, while The Texas Observer reported this month that Flores' signs have de-emphasized the Trump endorsement, part of a broader Republican trend.

As of Friday, the billboard remained standing despite the demand for removal; Gonzalez's campaign claimed Flores is "ashamed" of the president and the ICE raids, while BOLD PAC stated Flores is "paying lawyers to hide it."

Texas' 34th Congressional District remains a toss-up according to the Cook Political Report, though Trump would have carried it by about 10 points under new lines after Texas Republicans' mid-decade gerrymander.
title: Texas Republican Fights Billboard Touting Trump Ties

summary: On Friday, The White House announced that Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" after just five days, marking the shortest tenure in the position's history.

Scrutiny intensified following a 14-minute press conference Tuesday where Zacharia took only three questions, while the Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California regarding her lawyer claims.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia failed the bar exam; in an interview with Real America Voice, Zacharia claimed she "misheard" the question and deemed results "inconsequential" due to her work in China.

President Donald Trump advised Zacharia to "reconsider" the position, claiming the press treated her "unfairly" and "nastily," telling her, "Welcome to the world of Trump," two minutes before the announcement.

Zacharia praised Trump in a social media post, writing, "It was an honor to work for him," while Anthony Scaramucci, who served as White House communications director for 11 days, remarked that "records are made to be broken.
title: Zacharia speaks out after White House press secretary exit: ‘It was an honor’

bias: Coverage is primarily center-versus-right rather than left-versus-right: centrist framing emphasizes reported DNA collection, “sources,” legal context, and the potentially intrusive tactic of “dumpster diving,” while right-leaning accounts portray it as a widening criminal case tied to “immigration fraud,” “bombshell” evidence, and “likely coming indictments.” The center uses qualifiers such as “allegedly” and “potential,” whereas the right adopts urgency and suspicion through “stunning,” “raid,” and “far beyond.” The pivotal divide is whether discarded-trash DNA signals routine investigative procedure or escalating jeopardy.
Both emphasize the alleged search, DNA objective, raid, and broader probe, reflecting tensions over privacy, immigration, and partisan distrust.
summary: Federal agents reportedly searched discarded trash for DNA from Representative Ilhan Omar and her family before raiding Omar’s Washington, D.C., home, according to sources cited by NewsNation.
Homeland Security Investigations searched Omar’s residence on October 12, seized electronic devices, and conducted more than a dozen related searches, according to the reports.
The investigation includes some of Omar’s relatives, who reportedly received grand jury subpoenas as investigators reviewed immigration records for possible fraud or false statements.
Potential indictments could involve matters beyond publicly known allegations, with evidence expected to go before a grand jury.
title: Federal agents searched Omar’s trash for DNA before raid: Sources

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Marty O’Donnell’s forum as evidence of “white nationalist conspiracy theories,” racial hostility, and Nazi minimization, with terms like “slurs,” “Nazi talk,” and sometimes “rife with” heightening alarm.

Right-Leaning coverage offers little counter-narrative, largely repeating the same allegations rather than defending him, while center coverage adds electoral context—his challenge to Susie Lee—without resolving responsibility for members’ posts.
The pivotal divide is whether control of the forum implies political accountability, especially since authorship, moderation, O’Donnell’s response, and prevalence remain de-emphasized.
All perspectives emphasize his candidacy, forum control, and the AP’s review, reflecting broader disputes over extremism and accountability.
summary: An Associated Press review of thousands of posts on Nevada Republican congressional candidate Marty O'Donnell's online forum uncovered racial slurs, minimizations of Nazi Germany, and defenses of white nationalist conspiracy theories.

Long before his congressional run, O'Donnell gained fame as an award-winning 'Halo' video game composer whose fan forum he transformed into a campaign tool, referring to himself as its 'benevolent dictator.'

Extremist rhetoric permeated the site, with users asking 'Was Hitler really an evil guy?' and posting 'Heil Hitler,' which American University journalism professor Wendy Melillo identified as 'coded antisemitic hate speech.'

Campaign spokesman Keith Schipper stated O'Donnell 'has zero tolerance for hate' and the campaign 'dedicated a staffer to monitor' and remove individuals spewing vitriol, with nearly 200 users banned.

O'Donnell recently told a conservative outlet he was unaware of antisemitism 's resurgence, though he faced scrutiny earlier this year after hosting a far-right influencer with Nazi sympathies on his podcast.
title: Online forum controlled by Nevada GOP House candidate contains slurs and Nazi talk, AP review finds

bias: Left-Leaning coverage portrays Johnson’s polling dispute as “freaks out,” “frantic,” and “panicked,” framing optimism as defensiveness amid Democratic momentum and possible Republican losses.

Right-Leaning coverage recasts the same claims as confident resistance to “doom talk,” emphasizing a “hidden voter surge,” under-sampled Republicans, campaign crowds, and the prospect of “shock the pollsters,” while dismissing a “blue wave.” Center coverage presents an “optimist” confronting a potential “bloodbath,” balancing his faith and enthusiasm against unfavorable surveys.

All perspectives agree Johnson predicts retaining the House and disputes polling, but their divide reflects broader tensions over institutional credibility, populist skepticism, and electoral momentum.
summary: Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans will retain their U.S. House majority in the 2026 midterm elections despite Democratic momentum.
Johnson called predictions of a Democratic wave a “false narrative.”
Johnson and other Republican leaders questioned surveys showing Democrats could gain control of the House and possibly the Senate.
At a Texas rally, Johnson said he sees Republican support growing in swing districts that will decide the majority.
title: House Speaker Mike Johnson Draws on Faith as He Fights to Hold the Republican Majority

bias: The clearest contrast is tonal rather than ideological: left-associated framing uses “life and death,” “at stake,” and “most consequential” to stress historic consequences for diaspora communities, while right-associated coverage likewise highlights Jewish Americans’ substantial interest and “politically divided” response without clearly endorsing a distinct alternative or minimizing those stakes.
Center coverage adds sharper detail, describing political, religious, and generational divisions and presenting the vote partly as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu .

Across perspectives, “braces,” “contentious,” and “sharply divided” convey tension after three years of conflict, but headline evidence offers only weak support for firm left-right bias and no policy, polling, or candidate analysis.
summary: As the October 27 Israeli election nears, American Jews remain deeply divided along political and generational lines regarding Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's leadership.

Leading the Likud party, Netanyahu has served as prime minister for nearly 20 non-consecutive years, though his administration faces criticism for policies regarding the West Bank, Gaza, and expanding occupation.

Rabbi Dan Levin of Temple Beth El in Florida notes congregants are torn, while Orthodox congregant Stanley Weinstein believes Netanyahu has done "a terrific job," yet many share concerns regarding national unity.

Jason Isaacson, chief policy officer for the American Jewish Committee, notes substantial support for Israel remains in the United States despite controversy; many communities fear the election outcome could exacerbate domestic antisemitism.

The U.S. midterm elections scheduled for November 3 follow the Israeli vote by one week, with support for Palestinians and withdrawal of U.S. aid to Israel becoming rising issues among Democratic voters.
title: American Jewish Community Split Over Netanyahu as Israel Election Nears
